title: Who Owns a Language?
summary: Sociolinguistic argument on English as a lingua franca — inversion, complex noun phrases, stance markers.
text:
There are now considerably more people who speak English as an additional language than as a first one. Estimates vary, but by most accounts non-native users outnumber native users by something like three to one. Whatever the precise ratio, the consequence is the same: the majority of English conversations taking place at this moment involve no native speaker at all.

This has awkward implications for the idea of correctness. If two Brazilian engineers and a Korean project manager negotiate a contract in English, whose norms apply? The pragmatic answer is that they apply their own, and they usually succeed. Research on English as a lingua franca has repeatedly found that features which would be marked as errors in a classroom — a missing third-person s, a definite article where a native speaker would omit one — rarely cause misunderstanding. What does cause misunderstanding is unshared idiom, and idiom is disproportionately a native-speaker habit.

Not everyone welcomes this conclusion. One objection is practical: learners are still assessed by institutions that use native norms, so teaching anything else disadvantages them. This is a serious point, and it explains why most syllabuses remain conservative. Only when examination boards move will classrooms follow.

A second objection is that anything goes is not a teachable standard. But that is not what the research claims. The claim is narrower and more interesting: intelligibility, not nativeness, is the criterion — and intelligibility is an empirical matter that can be investigated rather than assumed.

Where does this leave the learner? In a stronger position than the traditional framing suggests. The goal is not to erase an accent or to pass as something one is not. It is to be clear, flexible and accommodating — qualities that, as it happens, many native speakers could usefully acquire as well.
